title: Personal Financial Literacy: Income, Scarcity, Spending, Credit and Saving
seo_title: Grade 3 Personal Financial Literacy Worksheets (TEKS 3.9, Texas)
standard_text: 3.9A explain the connection between human capital/labor and income; 3.9B describe the relationship between the availability or scarcity of resources and how that impacts cost; 3.9C identify the costs and benefits of planned and unplanned spending decisions; 3.9D explain that credit is used when wants or needs exceed the ability to pay and that it is the borrower's responsibility to pay it back to the lender, usually with interest; 3.9E list reasons to save and explain the benefit of a savings plan, including for college; 3.9F identify decisions involving income, spending, saving, credit, and charitable giving
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 personal financial literacy worksheets for Texas TEKS 3.9: income and human capital, scarcity and cost, planned and unplanned spending, credit and interest, saving plans and money decisions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Earn with skills, plan your spending, save for goals, and pay back what you borrow.
key_sub: Scarce things cost more. Credit is borrowing, and the borrower usually pays interest.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • Income is money earned by working. Skills and knowledge (human capital) can help people earn more.
  • When something is scarce, it usually costs more. When there is plenty of it, it usually costs less.
  • Planned spending is decided before you shop. Unplanned spending can leave less money for what you need.
  • Credit is borrowing. The borrower must pay the lender back, usually with interest.
  • A savings plan puts away money regularly for a goal, like college. People also decide how much to give to charity.

Examples

Example

Sam saves $6 a week for 9 weeks. How much does he save?

$6 × 9

Answer: $54

Example

Ava borrows $40 and pays $4 interest. How much does she pay back?

$40 + $4

Answer: $44

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Thinking credit is free moneyCredit must be paid back, usually with interest.
Thinking scarce things cost lessScarce means hard to get, so the price usually goes up.
Forgetting unplanned costsKeep some savings for surprises like a flat tire.

faq.q: What does personal financial literacy mean in Grade 3?
faq.a: Learning how people earn, spend, save, borrow and give money wisely (TEKS 3.9A to 3.9F).
The skills and knowledge a person has. Building them through school and practice can lead to higher income (TEKS 3.9A).
Borrowing money to pay for something now. The borrower must pay the lender back, usually with interest (TEKS 3.9D).
It helps you reach goals such as a bike or college by saving a set amount regularly (TEKS 3.9E).

items.q: Which is an example of planned spending?
c: Buying a toy you saw in a store window
Buying school supplies on a list made at home
Buying candy at the checkout because it looks good
Paying a fine for a late library book
items.e: Planned spending is decided before you shop, like a supply list.

items.q: Caleb has $25. He plans to spend $12 on a book. At the store he also buys a $3 snack that was not planned. How much money is left?
items.e: $25 − $12 − $3 = $10. The unplanned snack left him with $3 less.

items.q: Harper has $50. She plans to spend $31 on a book. At the store she also buys a $6 snack that was not planned. How much money is left?
items.e: $50 − $31 − $6 = $13. The unplanned snack left her with $6 less.

items.q: Which is an example of unplanned spending?

items.e: Unplanned spending happens without planning, like an impulse snack.
